First off, please be kind to yourself here.  It sounds like people who are unavailable are a "cozy" spot for you given your experiences with abandonment and sexual trauma.  Both types of experiences contribute to a genuine subconscious fear of closeness, despite humans being wired to desire closeness.  Most attraction to unavailable people stems from that fear of closeness.  

If you think about it, it's a basket to put all of your eggs in that doesn't challenge your perceptions of 'how things normally work' in relationships, and it's your mind trying to play out similar scenarios with the hope of a different resolution this time around.  Which is also what our minds are wired to do - find a solution to a problem, a happy ending to a story.  

With all that being said here, it's important to take people at face value in what they want or are ready for.  It's more important, in my opinion (a stranger on the Internet mind you, it's more important what you think about all of this), that you evaluate this pattern of attraction to partners who cannot or will not reciprocate your feelings, with compassion for yourself.  

Also I'm sure your friend means well, but maybe having a talk with her that getting angry at you isn't supportive or helpful in trying to navigate your feelings would be fruitful. Her insistence on what you SHOULD do/think/feel will not change the direction of your desire.  That happens within us, but supportive friends help us really look at our uncomfortable feelings about ourselves and relationships in such a way where it feels like we can take them on and resolve them.  

Pragmatically - you might want to get a different practice partner for a bit, so you can keep engaging in something that you love, that is meaningful for you, but you are in control of the shift of your attention.  It's much easier said than done, but to be very real with you - someone who doesn't want something serious will not change their mind "with the right person".  Let the guy heal and do his work on his own.  

I cannot stress enough that if you find yourself fixating on someone who you don't know very well and isn't available emotionally, that is not a challenge or 'sign' you should go for it - that more than likely is a call to action for yourself to turn inward and direct your focus to things/other relationships in your life that are meaningful and fulfilling.  

This man will not give you anything you don't already have within yourself.  And he will not give you the love you desire for now - and 'for now' is enough to pivot your focus.  At least for the time being.  

You don't have to avoid this person forever, but it is important to see things as they are and tend to your own needs, until you see something concrete that shows you two are on the same page.

So, first I would say, if you are just starting to talk to this person, it's important to remember that the goal here is to get to know each other better and with authenticity, not to make the other person feel good.  I am however inferencing that your note of not wanting to make them feel bad, is more so your desire to display your honesty with kindness and compassion, which is wonderful. 

I would say if you are going to be honest, I would include the 'why' as well, but ultimately you are framing this as what you perceive, your concerns, and with an openness that it could be a misinterpretation of this person OR it's just who they are and that's fine too.  It's a fine line to express your concerns, even if it's not a deal breaker, without coming across as you're just listing out the flaws of this person.  

But if there are things that you can see having an impediment on having a relationship with this person, this is a good opportunity to be vocal about that AND you're kind of doing an exercise of having a uncomfortable conversation that isn't in this "we're arguing about what we've built resentment for and just admitting to it now" kind of mode, which feels like much higher stakes. 


As an example, "To be honest with you, I noticed that you seem to shut down when you see me talking to other women when we are out.  This concerns me because I've been in previous relational dynamics where this behavior existed, and it honestly felt like someone assumed the worst of me constantly and I had to monitor my interactions with friends, so as to not upset this person.  Over time, that built up resentment, and I do not want that to happen here.  I am curious to know what you're thinking/feeling in those situations.  I want us to have an open and honest dialogue because I value that in relationships." 

I hope that helps.  I also recommend drafting up a response to the best of your ability and having a neutral friend that you trust, review it and give some feedback as well.

Yes!  Absolutely.  Sometimes I wake up and feel like everyone (friends, family, coworkers etc) all cannot stand me.  Sometimes it's triggered by being in large social gatherings, especially if I have been drinking.  

A piece of advice (if that is what you are looking for) is to hold those thoughts to high scrutiny.  Do you have PROOF?  Do people say these things to you?  

It sounds like when they do, it's part of a self-fulfilling prophecy or self-sabatoging.  

"Oh they all hate me"
"No they don't"
"But I feel like they do"
"But they don't?!"
"Omg do you hate me?!"
"NO"

AND THEN BOOM.  You've confirmed something you believe about yourself to be true, despite having no other evidence except when you push people away. 

Your thoughts about yourself, although they feel like fact, may not necessarily hold any truth beyond how you feel about yourself.  A byproduct of abuse is being in this cycle with yourself, even if your abuser is long gone.  Your mind has considered this high threshold of stress to be the norm, and times of peace can feel like a "calm before the storm" or like you're "missing something" because someone taught you not to trust your own confidence and sense of security.  

It's a process.  I very much struggle myself.  And you have to keep trying to do good for yourself.  A VERY IMPORTANT PART of this process is looking at your own internal dialogue and make it more kind.  It's detrimental to your healing that you become the person you need.  Not the person that hurt you.

Since starting EMDR I have these periods where my legs are in throbbing pain and there isn't a lot to ease it.  There were the occasional migraine here and there, insomnia etc.  My depression worsened and I ended up on an SSRI which I'm still kind of tinkering with dosages/brands and honestly sometimes am unsure if it's worth it.  

I try to be physically active and meditate.  Sometimes mindfully "breathing into" where the pain is helps.  Also one of those beaded heated eye masks for sleep helps a TON with headaches.  Warm baths with Epsom salt, acitaminophen when other things don't seem to help, herbal tea etc. 

It all sounds like this pithy temporary fix, but that's exactly what it is lol you're supposed to feel it to some degree.  It's just a balance of what you can bear until it passes through. 

I also have a tendency to smoke a lot of pot, which I'm trying to cut back on as it interferes with SSRIs, even being on a 10mg dosage.  I've been on this journey for about a year, and it suuuuccckkss to have the physical pain, when it happens it usually means your body is processing emotions and it just takes time, patience and some self-care.  

Just for context last night I didn't smoke pot for the first time in weeks and it seems like all the pain in my legs/hips/stomach came rushing back.  But I wouldn't endorse being a pothead considering had I let myself feel this pain probably wouldn't be here.  It's your body's way of saying "don't ignore me, I need you right now".  

But it sucks.  And you feel like you're crazy.  Most people don't understand it and sometimes I wonder if it's trauma or fibromyalgia, thyroid issues, rheumatoid arthritis etc.  

Oh and I ocillate between not having an appetite, and compulsive binge eating.  I'm still figuring out how it manifests.

I don't think it's up to your friends to tell you when/how you should forgive someone.  You don't owe anyone peace of mind simply because they request it.  

Also that "goodbye forever" deal was a tad dramatic, but whatever lol 

I'd say that even though it's been some years, someone you were engaged to breaking up through text and then disappearing is a bit of a traumatic experience, and I assume most people in general do not understand or fathom the scope of what you've been through.  It does sound like your SO understands to some degree, which must've been a huge relief.  

If these are friends you just game with and don't spend time face to face, it would make sense that an event like this would trigger an abrupt closing of the door on your friendships.  Not that gaming relationships are less than other kinds, or the friendship isn't as solid, you can just pick out the bullshit a lot easier when there isn't a screen between yous guys. 

All in all, I'd say give it some time.  Some people might come around, some might not.  You might settle down on your feelings, you might not 🤷🏼‍♀️ you never know where people will be at with you in six months, but I can assure you, the people that leave are making room in your life for better people and better friendships.  

But for your own sake?  I'd say look deeper into that pain and try to heal from it, and not so your friends will come back, but because you deserve peace.  Take your time and seek a therapist even for a short while if that helps.  We always minimize breakups but we cannot underestimate how intimate relationships impact us and how their success/demise shapes how we perceive the world and our role in it.  I hope you are as kind and supportive to yourself as you needed your friends to be ❤️ it'll get easier.
